title: Hosting, traveling, or staying in? How to keep pets happy this holiday season
text:

 Hosting, traveling, or staying in? How to keep pets happy this holiday season
 The holidays are full of good things: big meals, visits from loved ones, and cozy nights at home. They're also full of temptations and hazards that pets tend to find before their people do. 
 In a new Rover survey of U.S. pet parents, 63% say their pet has eaten holiday food it wasn't supposed to, and half have had a pet knock over the tree or chew on lights or decorations. For nearly 1 in 5 (18%), a forbidden snack ended in a trip to the vet. 
 The good news? Most of these mishaps are preventable. Here are five simple ways to keep the season safe, from the first feast to the last frost. 
 1. Set house rules for the holiday table 
 The season's first misstep often happens at the dinner table. More than 8 in 10 pet parents (82%) share scraps at least some of the time, so if your pet gets a holiday treat, keep it small and plain. 
 Safe in moderation: plain pumpkin, carrots, green beans, and unseasoned turkey breast with no skin or bones 
 Keep out of reach: cooked bones, chocolate, grapes, raisins, onions, garlic, and anything sweetened with xylitol 
 Ask guests not to share extras, and secure the trash after the meal. If your pet eats something toxic, call your vet or an animal poison control hotline right away, even if they aren't showing symptoms. 
 2. Deck the halls with pets in mind 
 Once the decorations go up, pets are just as curious about them as they were about the holiday dinner. Among those whose pets have tangled with holiday decor, more than half (54%) say it happened more than once. A few quick fixes can keep the tree standing: 
 Anchor the tree to a wall or ceiling hook. 
 Use cord protectors, and unplug lights when no one is home. 
 Hang shatterproof ornaments down low, and cover the tree stand's water. 
 Pick up ribbon, string, and wrapping paper right after gifts are opened. They can cause dangerous blockages if swallowed, especially in cats. 
 Cozy winter touches deserve a second look, too. Keep snow globes out of reach, since some are filled with antifreeze, and keep curious pets a safe distance from fireplaces and space heaters. 
 3. Guard the door 
 With parties come guests, and with guests comes an open door. Nearly half of pet parents (48%) say their pet has slipped out during a holiday gathering or come close, which is especially risky when it's cold outside. Before guests arrive, make sure your pet's ID tag and microchip info are current, and keep a recent photo on your phone. 
 Arrivals can be stressful, too. About 44% of pet parents say their pet hides, gets anxious, or acts protective around guests. To help ease this behavior, set up a quiet room with water, a bed, and a favorite toy before the doorbell starts ringing. 
 4. Plan holiday travel around your pet 
 The holidays are one of the busiest times of year to travel, which can make pet care harder to come by. Half of pet parents (50%) have shifted their travel dates or destinations, or canceled a trip altogether, because care wasn't available. When pets do come along, how they travel matters too: more than half of pet parents (55%) have chosen to drive instead of fly to keep their pet safe and comfortable. If you're hitting the road together: 
 Don't leave them alone in a parked car. Nearly 1 in 5 pet parents (18%) do this in winter, but a car can hold in cold the same way it holds in heat. 
 Check for cats before you start the engine. More than a third of pet parents (37%) never check or didn't know cats shelter near warm engines, so knock on the hood or honk first. 
 Pack paw wipes to clean off de-icing salt after stops. 
 If your pet is staying home, book care early and make sure your sitter has clear care instructions, your vet's number, and the location of the nearest 24-hour emergency clinic.
 Through Rover, pet parents can book sitters, walkers, and drop-in visits to keep routines steady while they're away. Plus, pet parents can add care instructions like feeding schedules, medications, and vet info right to their pet's profile in the app. Every care provider is background-checked, and verified reviews from other pet parents help you find the right fit. Every booking is also covered by the Rover Guarantee , so you can enjoy the holidays with a little extra peace of mind. 
 5. Know who to call 
 More than 4 in 10 pet parents (43%) say their pet has needed an emergency vet visit during the holidays. Before the season gets busy, check your vet's holiday hours, save the number for the nearest 24-hour emergency clinic, and keep an animal poison control hotline in your phone. 
 As temperatures drop, also watch for signs your pet has gotten too cold, like shivering, weakness, sluggishness, or pale or gray skin on the ears, tail, or paws. If you see them, move your pet somewhere warm and call your vet. 
 Most holiday surprises sneak up on pet parents, but a little prep now means more time for the good stuff: cozy nights, full bellies (the pet-safe kind), and plenty of snuggles. For holiday pet care you can count on, visit Rover or download the Rover app.
 Methodology: The Rover 2026 Winter Safety Survey was conducted by Pollfish among 1,000 U.S. pet parents on October 22, 2026.
